title: Database Sharding
intro: Replicas help with reads, but every replica still holds all the data. When the data or the writes outgrow one machine, you shard.

slides.heading: What is sharding?
slides.subtitle: Splitting data across databases.
slides.explain: Sharding splits a big table into pieces called shards, each on its own server. Each shard holds part of the rows, so no single machine stores or writes everything.
points: Each shard holds part of the data

slides.heading: The shard key
slides.subtitle: How rows are assigned.
slides.explain: The shard key decides which shard a row lives on, for example user_id. A good key spreads data evenly and keeps related data together.

slides.heading: Strategies
slides.subtitle: Ways to split the data.
slides.explain: Range sharding groups nearby keys, which is simple but can create hot spots. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly but makes range queries harder.
points: Range: IDs 1 to 1M on shard 1, and so on
Directory: a lookup table maps keys

slides.heading: The downsides
slides.subtitle: Sharding adds real complexity.
slides.explain: Queries across shards, like joins or global counts, become slow and complicated. Moving data when you add shards is also hard.

slides.heading: Before you shard
slides.subtitle: Try cheaper options first.
slides.explain: Indexes, caching, read replicas and bigger machines solve most problems. Sharding is usually the last step.
points: Shard when one machine truly can't cope

scenario.situation: A messaging app shards by country, putting each country's users on its own shard.
scenario.problem: One large country has most of the users, so its shard is overloaded while the others sit nearly idle.
scenario.fix: Re-shard by a hash of user_id. Users spread evenly across shards and the hot spot disappears.
scenario.takeaway: Pick a shard key that spreads load evenly.

cta: Have you ever had to shard a database?
